title: The `for` loop iterates through multiple values one by one in order and executes them.
when_to_show: When determining the output order or the number of iterations in a for loop
body: A `for` loop iterates through a collection of values—such as a list or a range—executing the same block of code repeatedly.
detail: When you write `for item in items:`, the values in `items` are assigned to the `item` variable one by one. The `print` statement inside the loop may be executed as many times as there are values. When studying this concept, you should check, in order, how many times the loop runs, the sequence in which the loop variable’s value changes, and whether string methods create new values or modify existing ones.

title: The `range()` function creates a sequence of numbers to iterate over.
when_to_show: When reading iteration ranges such as `range(3)` and `range(1, 4)`
body: The `range()` function generates a sequence of numbers commonly used in `for` loops. `range(3)` generates 0, 1, and 2 in sequence.
detail: `range(1, 4)` generates numbers starting from 1 up to but not including 4 (ending at 3). It is important to note that the end value is not included. When understanding this concept, you should check, in order: how many times the loop runs, the order in which the loop variable’s value changes, and whether a string method creates a new value or modifies an existing one.

title: During iteration, `append()` adds values to the list one by one.
when_to_show: When reading code that adds values to a list inside a `for` loop
body: When you use `append()` inside a `for` loop, a value is added to the list one at a time as the loop iterates.
detail: If you start with an empty list and write down what value is added in each iteration, you can predict the final list. Since `append` adds a value to the end of the list, the order is important. When studying this concept, you should check, in order: how many times the loop runs, the sequence in which the loop variable changes, and whether the string method creates a new value or modifies an existing one.

title: During iteration, the cumulative value reuses the previous value.
when_to_show: When reading cumulative calculations such as `total = total + n`
body: An accumulator variable generates a new value based on the previous value each time the loop iterates.
detail: The code `total = total + n` adds the previous `total` (on the right) to the current `n` and stores the result back in `total`. If you write down the `total` values for the first, second, and third iterations in order, you can see the final result. When studying this concept, you should check, in order: how many times the loop runs, the sequence in which the loop variable’s value changes, and whether the string method creates a new value or modifies an existing one.

title: `split()` splits a string into a list.
when_to_show: When reading code that converts a string separated by commas or spaces into a list
body: `split()` is a string method that splits a string into multiple pieces based on a specified delimiter and returns a list.
detail: `text.split(",")` splits the string at commas, while `text.split()` splits it at consecutive spaces by default. Since the result is a list rather than a string, subsequent code can utilize list-related constructs such as indices, `for` loops, `len`, and `append`. This method does not directly modify the original string.

title: strip() creates a new string with leading and trailing whitespace removed
when_to_show: When reading code that removes leading and trailing spaces from input values
body: The `strip()` function creates a new string by removing leading and trailing whitespace. It does not remove whitespace in the middle of the string.
detail: Since the value passed as `input` may contain accidental leading or trailing whitespace added by the user, `strip()` is often used before performing comparisons. When studying this concept, you should check, in order: how many times the loop runs, the order in which the loop variable’s value changes, and whether the string method creates a new value or modifies the existing one. Beginners often focus only on getting the final output correct and end up overlooking intermediate states.

title: The `replace()` method creates a new value by replacing a specific string with another string.
when_to_show: When reading code that replaces some characters in a string
body: `replace(old, new)` creates a new string by finding `old` within the original string and replacing it with `new`. For example, `'a-b'.replace('-', '')` replaces the hyphens with an empty string, resulting in `'ab'`.
detail: The original string itself is not automatically modified; you must store the result in a variable to use it later. When studying this concept, you should systematically verify how many times the loop runs, the order in which the loop variable’s value changes, and whether the string method creates a new value or modifies the existing one. Beginners often focus only on getting the final output correct and tend to overlook intermediate states.

title: The `lower()` and `upper()` functions convert text to lowercase or uppercase.
when_to_show: When reading code that checks for case sensitivity before comparing user input or strings,
body: The `lower()` function creates a new string with all characters in lowercase, and the `upper()` function creates a new string with all characters in uppercase.
detail: Since user input can come in various forms—such as “Yes,” “YES,” or “yes”—it is common to use `lower()` to standardize the input before comparison. When studying this concept, you should check, in order: how many times the loop runs, the order in which the loop variable’s value changes, and whether the string method creates a new value or modifies the existing one. Beginners often focus only on getting the final output correct and tend to overlook intermediate states.
